item.title: Phone subscriptions for internationals: What you need to know
item.description:
Partner content

Phone subscriptions for internationals: What you need to know

September 7, 2026

Whether you’ve just moved here or are looking to change your mobile phone provider, finding a phone subscription in the Netherlands can be a daunting task. So many advertisements! So many choices! So many requirements!

Sometimes, it seems as if you’re stuck in a Catch-22 situation: you need a BSN (Dutch social security number) to get a contract, but you often have to pay for it with a Dutch bank card. But to open a Dutch bank account, you will have to provide most banks with a BSN number (four banks in the Netherlands – ING, bunq, ABN Amro and Revolut – let you open an account without it, but you still have to provide them with a BSN number within 90 days).

To avoid this bureaucratic spiral, mobile service provider Simyo offers contracts without the usual required BSN number, giving you the option of moving beyond the prepaid plans most other companies offer to those without a BSN.

You can also use a foreign bank account to pay for your contract (although you must arrange that with customer service).

What’s the deal?

Simyo has been voted Best in Test by the independent Dutch consumer organization Consumentenbond for the second quarter of this year – its 38th time with that distinction.

Launched by telecom giant KPN some 20 years ago as an online-only mobile service provider, the budget Simyo uses KPN’s reliable 5G network, meaning you get excellent quality for a competitive price. (And if you have KPN internet and TV, you’ll get extra data at no charge.)

“Overall satisfaction with Simyo receives a 9.8 in the second quarter,” writes the Consumentenbond, which rates how satisfied customers are with their provider. Overall, Simyo got a rating of 8.2, “making it the Best in Test in during the second quarter of 2026.”

Specifically, says the Consumentenbond, “Customers report few outages regarding mobile internet and calling. They also experience few issues with slow connections. Administrative problems hardly occur. For example, about 1% reports a non-working SIM card, problems logging into the account, or an unjustified debit.”

Simyo’s mobile abonnement beat out Odido, Lebara and Vodafone/Ziggo, among others, in the consumer organization’s ratings.

À la carte pricing
Simyo offers both Sim Only and phone subscriptions that bear out its stellar quality to price ratio, with a Sim Only plan costing as little as €6,50 per month for the first year, increasing to €15 per month after 12 months. (And that includes Dutch taxes!)

For those looking for a subscription, plans offering 40 GB of data and 400 min/sms start for just €6,50 monthly (a temporary offer). You choose your plan à la carte, meaning you can decide how many minutes, gigabytes or months you’re looking for and the price will adjust automatically as you build your plan on Simyo’s website.

Buy a data cap
Don’t forget to take out the data cap for an additional €1 per month to save you from unexpected costs when your bundle runs out; your internet will then stop automatically when it reaches your limit.

Flexibility
Flexibility is another compelling reason to choose Simyo: monthly subscriptions allow you to adjust or cancel according to your needs and budget, doing away with those one- or two-year set contracts that lock you and your bank account in until they expire. That’s a huge advantage for internationals residing in the Netherlands for just a short period.

Data bundle
Simyo offers a data bundle for outside the EU that makes calling and internet surfing affordable while travelling.

eSIM cards
Simyo also offers eSIM (embedded SIM) cards that save you the hassle of inserting plastic chips, as you can download your mobile plan by scanning a code or using an app. You can manage your subscription via the user-friendly Mijn Simyo app.

“I wanted a second mobile number, for distant external contacts, to protect my main number,” wrote user Bert on Trustpilot, who gave Simyo a 5-star rating. “With an e-sim card from Simyo, I fixed that in 15 minutes, and it works fine.”

So if you’re looking for a new mobile phone plan, updating your old one or buying one for your teenage children, Simyo is an easy, affordable and reliable choice.

Click here to build your subscription today. It only takes minutes.

item.title: Netherlands must double water spending, delta commissioner warns
item.description:
Netherlands must double water spending, delta commissioner warns

September 7, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Netherlands must at least double what it spends on keeping the sea out and fresh water in, and even then it will not be able to prevent all the damage from climate change, delta commissioner Co Verdaas said on Monday.

Spending on flood defences, fresh water and climate-proofing currently amounts to about 1% of GDP, or just over €11 billion a year, and needs to rise to at least 2%, broadcaster NOS reported. His statements come ahead of the national budget day next week.

Verdaas gave a six-yearly review of the national delta programme to infrastructure minister Vincent Karremans. Carrying on as before “is not an option”, the infrastructure ministry said in a statement. The review stressed that the country is in “the next chapter of our water tradition.”

“We are world-renowned for our water management,” Verdaas said. “But this summer’s extremes have once again rubbed our noses in the facts. We are not going to make it with technology alone,” Verdaas said.

Pumps and salt
The review calls for billions of euros in new pumps at IJmuiden and, later, on the Afsluitdijk, so that river water can still be pushed out to sea as levels rise. NOS puts the IJmuiden works alone at around €2 billion. The pumping station protects some 4 million people, as well as Schiphol.

Preparations should also start now on new “Delta Works” to replace the Maeslantkering storm surge barrier near Rotterdam, and the IJsselmeer should be allowed to hold more water so it can keep supplying half the country in dry summers.

But technical fixes will not be enough, Verdaas said. Land use will have to change in the most vulnerable areas, including the bulb-growing Bollenstreek, the sandy soils of the east and south, the Noord-Holland coast and parts of Friesland and Groningen, where salt water is creeping in and farmers may have to change the crops they grow.

Households should expect “wet feet and flooded cellars” more often, the statement says, and hospitals and power installations will need extra protection from cloudbursts.

The findings follow a summer in which the Rhine fell to its lowest level in 80 years and the government formally declared a water shortage. The full Deltaprogramma 2027, with the revised strategy, is published on Prinsjesdag, September 15, alongside the budget.

item.title: Nazi’s daughter gives up looted Goudstikker painting
item.description:
Nazi’s daughter gives up looted Goudstikker painting

September 7, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The daughter of a Nazi official has given up all claim to a painting looted from the collection of Amsterdam art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, a year after it was spotted hanging above her sofa in photos on an Argentine estate agent’s website.

A federal judge in Mar del Plata approved a settlement on Friday in which Patricia Kadgien and her husband Juan Carlos Cortegoso can avoid trial for concealing the work, Argentinian media reported.

In return they have to each pay 2.4 million pesos, around €1,400, to a local mother and child hospital.

Portrait of a Lady now passes to Marei von Saher, Goudstikker’s daughter-in-law and sole heir, who has spent decades tracking down works from the collection. Her lawyers said she has agreed to let it go on show in Argentina before it is handed over, AP reported.

Estate agent’s photos
The painting had been missing since the war until August 2025, when AD journalists researching Kadgien’s father recognised it in photos of her house, which was for sale.

Friedrich Kadgien was financial adviser to Hermann Göring and fled to Argentina after the war. He died there in 1978 without ever being charged.

By the time police raided the house, the painting had gone and a tapestry of horses hung in its place. The couple were placed under house arrest and handed the work to prosecutors a week later.

Not a Ghislandi
The portrait of the Contessa Colleoni was catalogued by Goudstikker as the work of Giuseppe Ghislandi, but a court-ordered examination by Argentina’s national academy of fine arts concluded it was painted by Giacomo Ceruti, another 18th-century Italian, according to AP. Experts put its value at around $290,000.

Goudstikker died in May 1940 after falling into the hold of the ship carrying him away from the German invasion. Some 1,100 works from his stock were sold under duress to Göring and other senior Nazis, and the Dutch state returned 202 of them to his heirs in 2006.

item.title: Amsterdam canal swim raises record €3m for ALS research
item.description:
Amsterdam canal swim raises record €3m for ALS research

September 7, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

More than 3,300 people swam 2km through Amsterdam’s canals on Sunday and raised a record €3 million for research into the muscle-wasting disease ALS. Last year’s event brought in just under €1.73 million.

Swimmers set off from the Keizersgracht in groups every few minutes and finished at the Marineterrein, next to the maritime museum. A shorter 750-metre swim for children and less experienced swimmers took place earlier in the day.

Among the participants were 12 people who have ALS, some swimming under their own power and others towed through the water by family and friends. Television presenter Beau van Erven Dorens, radio host Marieke Elsinga, actress Monic Hendrickx and singer Maaike Ouboter also took part.

Hellespont origins
The event grew out of a 2011 fundraiser in which a group of friends swam the Hellespont in Turkey in memory of a friend who had died of ALS, raising €90,000.

The first Amsterdam edition followed in 2012, when some 1,100 swimmers, including the then Princess Máxima, raised €740,000.

ALS, or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, causes progressive loss of muscle control and has no cure. Most patients die within three to five years of their first symptoms. Around 500 people in the Netherlands are diagnosed every year, according to broadcaster NOS.

Donations remain open until the end of September and the final total will be announced on October 1.

item.title: Last taste of summer today before the rain sets in
item.description:
Last taste of summer today before the rain sets in

September 7, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Monday is set to be the last warm day for a while, with temperatures ranging from 24°C on the coast to as high as 29°C in Limburg and along the eastern border, according to the KNMI.

The weather service expects a fairly sunny afternoon with a brisk south-westerly wind, strong along the south-west coast. Cloud will build from the west in the evening, with a chance of a shower in places.

Change will come on Tuesday, when NOS weather forecasters expect highs of no more than 18°C or 19°C, lots of clouds and a lengthy spell of rain. Wednesday will also be cooler, with wind on both days.

Thursday should be drier, with temperatures around 20°C when the sun is out. Longer term, forecasters expect a mix of sunshine and showers at fairly average September temperatures, with no return of summer-like weather in sight.

Meteorological autumn began on 1 September.

item.title: Snapchat sued over addictive design in mass claim
item.description:
Snapchat sued over addictive design in mass claim

September 7, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A Dutch consumer foundation has filed a mass claim against the maker of Snapchat over the app’s “addictive” design, the second such case brought against the platform in the Netherlands in three months.

Consumer mass claims foundation SMC wants the court in Amsterdam to force Snap, Snapchat’s US parent company, to switch off features it says are built to keep users hooked unless a user deliberately turns them on.

It is also seeking compensation of between €425 and €1,850 per user, depending on how heavily and at what age they used the app.

In June, another foundation filed a similar case over Snapchat’s design and its use of personal data for advertising. A judge will decide which of the two can represent Dutch users.

Streaks and scores
Snapchat lets users send photos and messages that disappear after they’ve been viewed, and has more than 6 million monthly users in the Netherlands, who open the app around 40 times a day, according to figures cited by the foundation.

Features such as the “streak”, broken if two friends go a day without messaging, and the “snapscore”, which rises with use, pressure young people to keep coming back, SMC says. Internal Snap emails released in a US court case last year described the streak as “unintentionally addictive” and “fairly unhealthy”, the foundation said.

A Snap spokesperson told Algemeen Dagblad (AD) that the company remained committed to making Snapchat “a safe, positive and authentic place”, and that users valued streaks as a way to stay in touch. Snap said it had made it easy to pause and restore a streak, although restoring one costs €1 euro each time after a free first use.

SMC also wants Snapchat made safer for younger users, including curbs on location features it says allow strangers to find children, and action against accounts linked to drug dealing and grooming. Snap said location sharing on its map is off by default and that users have to choose to switch it on.

Under EU rules
The foundation argues the design breaches EU rules that require large platforms to protect users from addictive features. The European Commission has been investigating Snapchat over how it safeguards minors since 2025, and the Dutch consumer regulator (ACM) is examining the same question.

The case follows a US settlement last month in which Meta agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion and overhaul Instagram and Facebook for minors, a deal that named Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube as platforms expected to follow.

The first hearing is expected in about three months. Snapchat users, and parents acting for their children, can register for the claim free of charge on the foundation’s website.

item.title: Younger generations mostly richer than their parents: CBS
item.description:
Younger generations mostly richer than their parents: CBS

September 7, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Younger generations in the Netherlands have generally ended up with more spending power and more wealth than their parents and grandparents did at the same age, according to national statistics office CBS.

Home ownership, however, is an exception. The generation born between 1970 and 1985 is the most likely to own a home at age of life, CBS found. The number of 25- to 35-year-olds still living at home has also risen in recent years amid the housing shortage and rise in house prices.

The youngest adults are behind on wealth, too: up to around the age of 30, millennials and Generation Z hold less than earlier generations did at the same age, as more of them stay in education longer and start earning later.

Over a full lifetime, though, younger generations appear richer. Purchasing power rose almost continuously between 1977 and 2024, so at nearly every age people had more to spend than the generations before them.

At 45, for example, people born between 1970 and 1985 had average purchasing power of €44,100 in 2024 prices – around 40% more than the baby boomers had at the same age.

Wealth has followed the same path, lifted mainly by rising house prices before falling back more recently with a rise in inflation. Millennials had the sharpest rise in their 30s of any generation.

Younger generations also spend a smaller share of their income on housing, CBS said, and are more likely to live in a flat.

item.title: Dutch schools must make space for languages spoken at home
item.description:
Dutch schools must make space for languages spoken at home

September 7, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch primary schools are now expected to make room for the languages pupils speak at home, like Turkish, Polish and Arabic. New national curriculum standards will encourage teachers to allow students to use their mother tongue to prepare for class or better understand material if it helps them.

The change comes from updated core objectives (kerndoelen) for the Dutch language, which became law in August and set out what children are meant to learn. Current affairs programme Nieuwsuur reported on the new rules on Friday.

About a quarter of people aged 15 and over mainly speak something other than standard Dutch at home – a dialect, a regional language such as Frisian or Limburgish, or another language such as English, Turkish or Polish, according to the national statistics office CBS.

What the schools actually do with the new standards is largely up to them. Attention to multilingualism and pupils’ linguistic identity is obligatory, but the more concrete idea – letting children talk through difficult material in their home language, or prepare for a lesson in it – is advice rather than a strict requirement.

Not everyone agrees
Language expert Joanneke Prenger, who advises on primary education, said parents should “speak the language you know best” with their children, reversing years of guidance to use Dutch at home. Doing so, she told Nieuwsuur, gives pupils a richer base for learning Dutch and other languages.

Thomas Hendriks, who teaches Dutch in an Amsterdam bridging class for pupils with a language gap, said the steady stream of new advice “comes across as a whim, a trend”, even as more young people leave school unable to read and write properly. In his classroom, he added, letting pupils switch languages also means losing track of what is being said.

The debate comes amid years of concern about basic Dutch skills. The Netherlands was once seen as a strong performer in reading, but scores have fallen sharply, and a national programme worth hundreds of millions of euros has yet to turn things around.

A tougher line elsewhere
The classroom shift runs alongside a harder line on Dutch in other areas. Ministers want to raise the language level required for naturalisation to B1, and are drawing up stricter rules for welfare claimants who do not speak adequate Dutch.

For international families, the change means a child’s English, Turkish or Polish is now something schools are meant to work with rather than discourage. Regional languages count too – Friesland already requires schools to actively teach Frisian.

Schools have until 2031 to fold all the new objectives into their teaching, and for now decide for themselves how to handle home languages.

item.title: The Hague’s historic jenever distillery is fighting for its life
item.description:
The Hague’s historic jenever distillery is fighting for its life

September 6, 2026 Brandon Hartley

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The iconic Van Kleef Distillery dates back to 1776. It’s faced countless challenges since then, but the latest round could force it to close or substantially change.

For over two centuries, the Van Kleef Distillery in The Hague has been mixing up unique liqueurs and genever made with time-tested recipes. Vincent van Gogh is one of the customers known to have sampled its spirits.

Despite its rich history and status as the last remaining distillery in the city, owner Fleur Kruyt says Van Kleef is currently facing a series of setbacks that could shut down its long-time location on the Lange Beestenmarkt.

“Right now I have the same colour hair as my grandmother at the age of 96,” she told DutchNews during an interview in the distillery’ tasting room.

Kruyt has spent the past several years trying to come up with solutions to appease her landlord and city officials as she strives to expand Van Kleef’s operations, modernise its museum, and, more than anything else, prevent its doors from closing altogether.

It’s all enough to turn the hair of even the most steadfast and indomitable of small business owners completely white.

But these challenges are only the latest in Van Kleef’s tumultuous history. Over the years, it’s contended with the sudden death of an owner, a crime wave, overzealous safety inspectors, and the Covid pandemic.

The first few centuries
The distillery dates all the way back to the late 18th century. It originally opened in 1776 as Distilleerderij “Anker” before being taken over by the Van Kleef family in 1842.

Kruyt is convinced Van Gogh stopped by at least once. The famous artist may have even been a regular given his proclivities. He lived down the street from 1869 to 1873 and spent those years working at Goupil & Cie, an art business in The Hague owned by his uncle.

Along with the rest of the Netherlands, the distillery managed to endure the impacts of the Spanish flu pandemic and two World Wars, but it was a safety inspection in 1986 that came much closer to shutting it down.

Explosive concerns
The officials declared the 40,000 litres of alcohol sitting in the distillery’s vats were a huge safety risk that made it an almost literal ticking time bomb. They decided it was no longer safe to distill alcohol on the property.

At the time, Van Kleef was teetering on the edge of bankruptcy. The surrounding neighbourhood was considered a “no-go zone” for many of the city’s residents and the distillery wasn’t getting much foot traffic.

“If you walked these streets as a woman at night back then, you were either a prostitute or tired of your life,” Kruyt said. “There was lots of criminality. No one came here anymore.”

After much discussion and planning, production was moved off site. The building itself was purchased by a local development company called Stadsherstel Den Haag and Van Kleef officially became a tenant in its long-time home.

The books were eventually balanced after it attained historical status and Van Kleef finally reopened as a multipurpose operation in 1995. Along with the museum and a tasting room, Van Kleef’s liqueurs are bottled and labelled there to this day.

Even more setbacks
The construction of a tram tunnel and the redesign of the street out front dragged on for over a decade and further drove customers away.

The distillery’s revenue dropped by 80% when the city began installing barriers around the neighbourhood to discourage auto traffic in 2009. Its suppliers and customers had to navigate a maze every time they tried to go there.

Kruyt, who was operating Van Kleef with her husband Louis Centazzo at the time, was forced to use their house as collateral on a loan to keep it open. Then he suddenly died in 2015, leaving her to manage the distillery on her own.

Foreclosure followed and Kruyt moved into an apartment on the property. The hits kept coming as gentrification quickly transformed the neighbourhood and raised the distillery’s monthly rent along with it.

Then the Covid crisis began, which forced Van Kleef to shut down its tasting room. Undaunted, Kruyt and her crew came up with clever ways to ensure revenue would keep coming in.

She joked that “booze was declared a necessity” during the pandemic. Kruyt developed a “vaccine” after inspiration struck while she was giving her dog injections for arthritis. “The Van Kleef Vaccine” is a mix of Limoncello, Vitamin C, and ginger-infused liqueur.

At first, Kruyt fretted that it wouldn’t go over well with customers who had spent weeks social distancing and worrying they’d be the next ones to catch Covid. Those fears proved unfounded.

“And the first people who bought it? Doctors and pharmacists,” she recalled. “They found it really cool. I thought, ‘If these people find it funny, I don’t care about the rest!’”

A “ginitiser” sold in spray bottles soon followed. It, too, was a hit.

The current dilemmas
“We’ve always managed and, whenever I feel bad, I turn on the television and see how it could be a lot worse,” Kruyt said before discussing the latest round of threats to the distillery.

The city’s decision to impose a flat €50-a-day parking fee has taken another bite out of Van Kleef’s revenue. The policy was so controversial it was even covered by The Guardian in 2023. If all this wasn’t enough, Kruyt broke her ankle while on a summer holiday and the recovery process required several surgeries.

Determined to keep the distillery where it’s been for over 200 years, Kruyt has been combating another wave of financial woes coupled with bureaucratic headaches, soaring energy bills, and other increased costs. Even the price of the glass that goes into Van Kleef’s bottles has gone up recently.

A crowdfunding campaign has been underway since 2025. Plans were also made to expand operations to attract more visitors, but negotiations with Stadsherstel Den Haag have proven challenging.

After over two years of discussions about everything from the future of the museum to renovations for the apartments on the property, Kruyt said the situation has been handed over to a new director named Jan-Willem de Bruijn.

“Stadsherstel Den Haag is currently taking a comprehensive look at the complex,” De Bruijn told DutchNews. “This means that, in addition to the shop and the tasting room, we are also focusing on the redevelopment of the museum and garden as well as upgrades in the apartments. In doing so, we aim to invest sustainably in the preservation of this unique and characteristic part of The Hague.”

Delays with permitting haven’t helped. DutchNews contacted the office of Alderwoman Saskia Bruines for comment about this and other matters concerning the distillery, but had not received a response as of press time.

Fighting onward
Regardless of what happens next, Kruyt says Van Kleef will continue in one form or another, even if that means turning it into a distillery-and-wholesaler-only operation at a facility closed to the public and likely located on the outskirts of The Hague.

“But all of this history would go away,” she said as she gestured towards the centuries-old equipment in Van Kleef’s museum.

Takeaway liqueurs and tastings have covered the costs of maintaining the distillery’s historical inventory, but the current circumstances have made that impossible to continue. As Kruyt faces another round of discussions with Stadsherstel Den Haag, she’s determined to stay optimistic.

“We met with Jan-Willem a few weeks ago,” she said. “We’re really happy that he is taking everything seriously and trying to preserve the heritage that we have here.”

Still open for business
Visitors to Van Kleef can currently visit the small museum, enjoy drinks and snacks in its tasting room, host gatherings in a former storage cellar turned conference room, and purchase bottles of liqueurs made with recipes that date back to the 17th century.

Among them is Bridal Tears, which contains flakes of 24-carat gold. It was once a popular wedding gift. The bawdy tales and traditions surrounding it and two accompanying liqueurs could fill an entire book.

In an age of alcoholic beverages with preservatives and other ingredients that are difficult to describe, let alone pronounce the names of, Van Kleef is still doing things the old-fashioned way.

“All of our recipes have been preserved,” Kruyt said. “We have an archive full of them that began in the 1840s. Everything you’re tasting is real in the sense that there’s no artificial flavouring or colourings.”

The distillery continues to attract international visitors and aficionados of liqueurs. Kruyt said a few of them are household names, but she demurred when asked for the details.

“What happens at Van Kleef, stays at Van Kleef,” she said. “So any celebrities out there, you can come here and we won’t talk about you.”

item.title: The Many Lives of Anne Frank: a fascinating work
item.description:
The Many Lives of Anne Frank: a fascinating work

September 5, 2026 Molly Quell

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Many Lives of Anne Frank is a biography, of the German Jewish teenager herself, of her famous diary and, also, of her legacy. Ruth Franklin’s innovative approach to the most famous work of the Holocaust is fascinating, thought-provoking and well worth the read.

The Diary of Anne Frank has been assigned to thousands of students and has sold millions of copies. The annex where the teenager hid with her family during the Second World War is visited by a million tourists a year, whose queue snakes along the canal in Amsterdam for blocks.

Published in 2025, the first half of the book is a classic biography. We follow the Frank family from Germany to exile in the Netherlands and then to further banishment above a warehouse on the Prinsengracht. Franklin brings the story to life, with minute details (it was raining on the evening the Franks walked across the Dutch capital to their hiding place) and wider context (the ongoing round-up of Jews by the occupying Nazis.)

The biography does not end, as most biographies do, with the subject’s death. The young girl died somewhere in March or April of 1945 at Bergen-Belsen concentration camp, possibly just weeks before it was liberated by the British army.

Her legacy lives on, in her diary published, following edits from her father, shortly after the war. Anne herself also edited the work, inspired by a 1944 appeal from the Dutch minister for education diaries and letters documenting the German occupation. The teen aspired to get her thoughts and feelings into print.

The second half of the book follows the legacy of the diary, how it came into being and how it became a phenomenon, vaulting Anne Frank to an epic level of fame.

Franklin delves into the details of the book’s publication journey, raising questions about what it means for something to be “authentic.”

Anne’s father Otto sends a translated (and edited) version to relatives in Switzerland, who encourage him to publish the work. A composite of Anne’s two versions, plus her father’s edits is submitted to a publisher, who suggests certain cuts as to not offend more conservative readers. A longer, critical edition was published in 1986 and, based on that, the English-language version was published in 1989.

The first German-language version edits a passage Anne wrote taking a dig at the country. She writes “Only civilized languages are permitted [in the Annex], therefore no German,” which is changed to “all civilised languages may be spoken.” The occupants made an effort to speak to one another in Dutch, rather than in their native German, as a form of resistance.

The chapters are all titled with descriptors of the various versions of Anne. The final one is called “Pawn” and addresses her legacy. Otto intended for the diary to “promote peace and tolerance,” Franklin writes, but he couldn’t control his daughter’s celebrity.

The adaptation of the diary in a play in the United States is complicated by differing artistic versions of the work, the iconic image of Anne is used by those protesting South African apartheid and later, Israel’s war on Gaza. Franklin’s chronicle leaves the reader with many questions about how to contextualise the diary of a teenage girl.

A prize-winning literary critic, Franklin is a former editor at The New Republic. Her first biography, Shirley Jackson: A Rather Haunted Life, won multiple awards. The Many Lives of Anne Frank was a finalist for the 2025 Los Angeles Times Book Prizes.

The Many Lives of Anne Frank is deeply researched, well-written and stimulating.

You can get your copy at the American Book Center.
